query: For refractory high-entropy alloys intended for structural use under extreme-temperature conditions, what single intervention could improve high-temperature oxygen resistance? State one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to the untreated alloy, defines the temperature, atmosphere, and exposure conditions under which it should work, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment with a clear result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Increasing the aluminum content in a refractory high-entropy alloy will enhance its high-temperature oxygen resistance by promoting the in situ formation of a continuous, adherent alumina (Al2O3) scale.
generation.material_initial_state: A refractory high-entropy alloy composed of refractory elements in near-equimolar ratios with baseline low aluminum content designed for structural applications at extreme temperatures.
generation.intervention: A controlled compositional modification to increase the aluminum content in the alloy.
generation.conditions: Exposure to air (≈0.21 atm O2) at 1100–1200°C for 100 hours.
generation.structural_mediator: Development of a dense, slow-growing, and adherent Al2O3 scale on the alloy surface.
generation.mechanism: The elevated aluminum content is expected to oxidize preferentially to form a thermodynamically stable alumina layer that serves as a diffusion barrier to oxygen, thereby reducing further oxidation of the alloy substrate.
generation.predicted_outcome: A reduction of at least 50% in oxidation weight gain compared to the untreated (lower aluminum) alloy, along with improved scale adherence and fewer spallation events.
generation.baseline: The untreated refractory high-entropy alloy with standard aluminum content, which exhibits higher oxidation weight gain and less protective oxide scale formation under the same high-temperature conditions.
generation.boundary: The predicted improvement is expected under high-temperature oxidation conditions (1100–1200°C in air for 100 hours); effects under different temperatures, atmospheres, or shorter exposure times remain uncertain.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal aluminum concentration for maximal protective oxide formation, as well as potential interactions with other alloying elements that might affect scale adhesion and growth kinetics, needs further clarification.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of refractory high-entropy alloy samples: one with the standard (baseline) aluminum content and one with an increased aluminum content. Subject both sets to oxidation testing at 1100–1200°C in air for 100 hours. Post-exposure, assess the oxidation weight gain and analyze the surface scales using XRD and SEM/EDS.
measurements: Phase identification of the oxide scale (presence and continuity of Al2O3) using XRD
Microstructural characterization of the scale adhesion and morphology via SEM/EDS
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the increased aluminum alloy does not show a statistically significant reduction (≥50%) in oxidation weight gain relative to the baseline alloy or if the expected continuous, protective Al2O3 scale is not observed (as confirmed by XRD and SEM/EDS), then the hypothesis will be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: This paper utilizes in situ X-ray diffraction (XRD) to investigate the high-temperature oxidation behaviour of CrMnFeCoNi high-entropy alloy (HEA). We found that (1) Mn is the major oxide-forming element in both vacuum and air environments, leading to the formation of non-protective oxides that deplete the bulk alloy of Mn; (2) no oxides like Cr 2 O 3 , Fe 2 O 3 , or Fe 3 O 4 were observed during the high-temperature oxidation behaviour of CrMnFeCoNi, which contradicts some previous studies on the isothermal oxidation of CrMnFeCoNi HEA. We also analysed and compared the experimental results with thermodynamic calculations by using ThermoCalc version 2022b software following the CALPHAD method. ThermoCalc predicted spinel oxide in a vacuum environment, along with halite oxides observed in experimental results; also, in an atmospheric environment, it predicted only spinel, indicating the need for further investigation into factors to validate the thermodynamic predictions. Our study shows that the in situ HTXRD technique is a powerful tool to accurately identify time–temperature-dependent phase formation/transformation for studying oxidation behaviours and understanding oxidation mec

Abstract Although refractory high entropy alloys (RHEAs) have shown potentials to be developed as structural materials for elevated temperature applications, most of the reported oxidation behaviours of RHEA were associated with short term exposures for only up to 48 hours, and there is a lack of understanding on the oxidation mechanism of any RHEA to-date. In this work, by using thermogravimetric analysis, isothermal oxidation was conducted on a novel RHEA at 1000 °C and 1100 °C for up to 200 hours, which is an unprecedented testing duration. The external oxide layer strongly influenced the weight gain behaviours, and it consisted of CrTaO 4 -based oxide with some dispersion of Al 2 O 3 and Cr 2 O 3 . At 1000 °C, the inability to form dense CrTaO 4 -based oxide layer resulted an exponential dependence of weight gain throughout 200 hours. At 1100 °C, mass gain curve showed two parabolic dependences associated with the formation of protective CrTaO 4 -based oxide layer and the weight gain after 200 hours was 4.03 mg/cm 2 , which indicates that it is one of the most oxidation resistant RHEAs comparing to literature data to-date. chosen.technique: high-temperature furnace oxidation tests coupled with post-exposure microstructural and phase analysis (e.g., XRD and SEM/EDS)
chosen.conditions: Target tests performed at 1100–1200°C under atmospheric oxygen (≈0.21 atm O2) for 100-hour exposures
chosen.why: This move directly addresses the open question by proposing a single, compositional intervention – namely, a controlled increase of aluminum – to induce the in situ formation of a protective, slow-growing alumina scale. Prior studies on conventional high-temperature alloys have demonstrated that alumina scales significantly enhance oxidation resistance. By eliminating simplified assumptions in earlier work and explicitly quantifying the mitigation (e.g., a ≥50% reduction in oxidation weight gain compared to untreated alloys), the study hypothesis is clearly testable, with the oxidation kinetics and microstructural evolution serving as falsifiable indicators.
